Definition: from G5306; to be later, i.e. (by implication) to be inferior; generally, to fall short (be deficient):--come behind (short), be destitute, fail, lack, suffer need, (be in) want, be the worse.
BiblicalUsage: hysteréō turns up where the Bible says to come short, to lack, to be in need. In Matthew 19:20, the text says "what lack I yet?" In Mark 10:21, the text says "One thing thou lackest."
TheologicalSignificance: For me, hysteréō is a reminder that God provides, and His provision is enough — even when it does not look like we expected. That shapes how I read the passages where it appears: not as filler, but as God's own wording for what He is doing.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana; The Rich Young Ruler
